result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.which_multiple()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find edge IDs of multiple edges (duplicate edges between same node pairs). ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L23169-L23231){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.which_multiple() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} Returns a list of edge IDs that represent multiple/duplicate edges. These edges share the same source and target nodes as another edge in the graph. This is useful for detecting and cleaning multigraphs. For undirected graphs, edges `(u,v)` and `(v,u)` are considered the same pair. When multiple edges exist between a pair, all edge IDs (including the first) are returned. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of edge IDs representing multiple edges. Empty if no duplicates exist. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} - self-loops are not considered multiple edges (use `which_loops()` instead) - in undirected graphs, (u,v) and (v,u) are treated as the same pair - returns all edges involved in duplication, including the first occurrence - useful for data quality checks before analysis ## Examples {.doc-examples} Adding the same edge more than once creates duplicates; every occurrence of a duplicated pair is returned, including the first: ::: {#f1f2f70e .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph(directed=True) g.add_node(label="Alice") g.add_node(label="Bob") g.add_node(label="Carol") g.add_edge(source="Alice", target="Bob", weight=1.0) g.add_edge(source="Alice", target="Bob", weight=2.0) # Duplicate connection g.add_edge(source="Alice", target="Bob", weight=3.0) # Another duplicate g.add_edge(source="Bob", target="Carol", weight=1.0) # Single edge # Returns 3 (all Alice -> Bob edges) len(g.which_multiple()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 3 ``` ::: ::: A simple graph with no repeated connections has no multiple edges, which makes this a quick way to validate graph simplicity: ::: {#0336edc4 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_node(label="A") .add_node(label="B") .add_node(label="C") .add_edge(source="A", target="B") .add_edge(source="B", target="C") .add_edge(source="C", target="A") ) # Returns True: no duplicate edges len(g.which_multiple()) == 0 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` True ``` ::: :::
